newsitem.title: USA: NATO candidates not eager to buy costly new arms.
newsitem.headline: NATO candidates not eager to buy costly new arms.

text.p: Western arms makers, eager for a piece of a new multibillion-dollar market, are hawking their wares to prospective new NATO members in Europe.

Former Communist states Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, expected to get invitations to join NATO at a Madrid summit next week, have put a higher priority on financial stability and consumer happiness than on $20 million fighter jets.

But pressure for military "compatibility" among alliance members means rich contracts in coming years, starting with modest items like radios and hose connections for fuel lines but extending to aircraft and armour.

Joel Johnson, vice president for international affairs at the U.S. Aerospace Industries Association trade group, said it was impossible to estimate the value of the new market but said warplane buys alone might total more than $10 billion.
"There is a big market," Johnson said, adding that U.S. and competing aircraft firms wanted to get initial orders because those were usually followed by later purchases.
"But how fast these countries manage to buy and absorb will only be as fast as their economies develop, rather than measuring any threat," he cautioned.
Arms manufacturers from the United States, Britain, France, Sweden and other countries, including Russia, have been touring central Europe.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be invited to join at Madrid. Some European countries also would like Romania and Slovenia in but that is opposed by the United States, which sees them joining in a second wave.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Tuesday defended Western pressure for the new democracies to upgrade their militaries to fulfil NATO requirements for a common defence.

"Whether or not countries are admitted into NATO, these countries will have to modernise their defensive capabilities in any event," Cohen told reporters at a photo opportunity with visiting Swedish Defence Minister Bjorn Von Sydow.
"One cannot expand NATO and not ask those new members of NATO to carry their full measure of support for the requirements. So they will have to measure up," he said.
Sweden is a nonaligned country, but Von Sydow said a consortium of SAAB and British Aerospace PLC "can offer a very cheap and efficient aircraft fighter" to buyers.

Warsaw, Budapest and Prague, armed with old Soviet equipment and bloated forces, do not rule out Russian upgrades or leasing Western jets now while focusing on anti-aircraft missiles, communications and other basics.
"This will be an enormous expense for us," Marek Dukaczewski, undersecretary in Poland's National Security Bureau, told Reuters of Warsaw's need for new weaponry, including some 100 fighters.

The Saab-British Aerospace consortium is offering the JAS-39 Gripen fighter, while U.S. giants Lockheed Martin Corp. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., with the F-16C and F-18 respectively, are in the race along with France's Mirage 2000-5, made by Dassault Aviation.
Dukaczewski cautioned that any acquisitions from the West will have to be weighed against a possible decision to simply update Poland's Soviet-made MiG-29s, MiG-23s and SU-22s.

Like other East European states, Poland has a large army with old equipment and redundant Warsaw Pact facilities which consume much of the available money needed for modernisation. It is unlikely to begin making decisions on major purchases until a 15-year military restructuring plan is ready.

The Czechs now spend 2 percent of gross domestic product on defence, and that is expected to remain flat or drop to about 1.9 percent under 1997 projections. Czech officials say they have the will, but not the wallet, to buy new fighters but are keeping options open.
The U.S. Navy has offered to lease them seven used F-18s under a no-cost, five-year agreement but Lockheed-Martin, the Swedish-British consortium and the French are all competing to provide aircraft.

Hungary's biggest arms purchase on the horizon is the replacement of its ageing MiG-21 and MiG-23 fighters, which fly alongside the country's 28 more modern MiG-29s. The deal, estimated at $1 billion, would involve buying some 30 planes.
In addition to Western firms, Russia has offered MiG-29s and SU-39s and both Russia and Israel have offered an even cheaper alternative of upgrading 30 MiG-21s for $150 million to $200 million.
Hungary recently announced that a $100 million tender for shoulder-launched anti-aircraft missiles was won by France's Matra Defence.

Slovenia has made no public announcement on purchases, but Romania intends to buy 100 advanced jets and says it will go ahead with a $1.5 billion deal to buy NATO-compatible helicopters even if it is not invited in the first wave.
